summary: This Wikipedia article summarizes the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil. It covers the qualified teams, the 64 matches in 12 host cities, and new officiating technology used for the first time. It also describes the group-stage and knockout results, including the 7-1 semi-final win over Brazil by Germany, and the final in which Germany beat Argentina 1-0 to win its fourth title.
one_line: Overview of the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, including its teams, venues, technology, results, and Germany's 1-0 final win over Argentina.
key_facts: Thirty-one national teams qualified through qualification competitions to join host nation Brazil in the final tournament, with Bosnia and Herzegovina as the only debutant.
A total of 64 matches were played in 12 venues located in as many host cities across Brazil.
For the first time at a World Cup finals, match officials used goal-line technology and vanishing spray for free kicks.
FIFA Fan Fests in each host city gathered a total of 5 million people.
Brazil received 1 million visitors from 202 countries during the tournament.
Every World Cup-winning team since the first tournament in 1930 (Argentina, Brazil, England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Uruguay) qualified for the 2014 tournament.
Spain, the title holders, were eliminated at the group stage, along with England and Italy.
Uruguay were eliminated in the round of 16, and France exited in the quarter-finals.
Host nation Brazil, which had won the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup, lost 7-1 to Germany in the semi-finals and finished in fourth place.
In the final, Germany defeated Argentina 1-0 to win the tournament.
Germany's 1-0 win in the final secured the country's fourth world title and was its first since German reunification in 1990.
West Germany also beat Argentina in the World Cup final when it won the title before reunification.
Germany became the first European team to win a World Cup staged in the Americas.
The result marked the first time nations from the same continent won three consecutive tournaments, following Italy in 2006 and Spain in 2010.
